title: A camera in every room needs a network
subtitle: A health system puts cameras, microphones and edge AI in hundreds of patient rooms for virtual nurses and fall alerts, on switches and Wi-Fi sized for badge readers and phones.

today.title: Rooms go live faster than closets
today.exec: Each smart room adds a camera, microphone and screen, and the rollout is planned by the nursing project, not against switch power or uplink capacity.
today.dir: Nobody holds one list of which rooms are live, which switch ports feed them and how much PoE budget is left in each closet.
today.eng: Room devices draw PoE and send continuous video to an edge node or cloud, so port power class, uplink headroom and QoS marking decide picture quality.

today.title: The virtual nurse sees a frozen picture
today.exec: When video stalls, the virtual nurse loses sight of the patient and the bedside nurse is called back, which is the workload the program was meant to remove.
today.dir: The camera vendor, the network team and the video platform each check their own console, and each reports healthy.
today.eng: Symptoms span switch PoE events, Wi-Fi roaming, QoS re-marking at the distribution layer and the vendor's cloud relay, with no shared timestamped trace.

today.title: A fall alert arrives late or never
today.exec: A fall alert that depends on an overloaded closet or a stalled edge node can arrive late, and a correct alert still fails if staff cannot arrive.
today.dir: Privacy questions land at the same time: who can view a room, what is recorded and where frames leave the building.
today.eng: Without per-room health checks, an inference node that has stopped processing looks identical to a quiet room.

withCisco.title: One view from room to cloud
withCisco.exec: Operations asks one question and sees room devices, switch power, wireless health and the vendor's cloud path together on one canvas.
withCisco.dir: AI Canvas in Cloud Control would pull Meraki or Catalyst Center port and PoE data, ThousandEyes path tests and Splunk events into one investigation.
withCisco.eng: Topology and Inventory would map each room device to its switch port and closet, with ThousandEyes tests to the vision vendor's endpoints and device logs in Splunk.

withCisco.title: Nursing informatics approves the change
withCisco.exec: Before any switch or QoS change reaches patient rooms, named network and nursing approvers see the proposed change, the rooms affected and the rollback.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the change until it is approved, and the Audit log would record who approved what and when.
withCisco.eng: The approved change (PoE priority, QoS policy or port move) is pushed by Catalyst Center or the Meraki dashboard, not by the agent directly.

withCisco.title: Modeled: faster isolation, same clinical questions
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: the fault is located in one investigation instead of a multi-team call; whether virtual nursing reduces workload or falls is not something the network settles.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes room devices, switches and the vendor path are all onboarded; rooms on unmanaged switches stay invisible.
withCisco.eng: Camera firmware, model accuracy and the vendor's cloud remain outside Cisco telemetry except as measured from the network edge.

approval.title: Change to patient-room switch ports
approval.what: Raise PoE priority and apply the video QoS policy on the closets serving one unit's smart rooms.
approval.approver: Network change manager with the nursing informatics lead
approval.executesIn: Catalyst Center or the Meraki dashboard

ask: If a virtual nurse's video froze tonight, who would know first, and how long before you knew whether it was the camera, the closet or the vendor's cloud?
stays: Clinical protocols, consent and privacy policy, camera placement and the vision vendor's model accuracy stay with the hospital and its vendor.
caveat: Evidence is mixed: 57% of surveyed nurses saw no workload relief, and a 2026 matched study found no significant fall reduction. Cisco tooling addresses the infrastructure path only; the outcome shown is modeled, not measured.

title: When the phone agent cannot reach the EHR
subtitle: A voice agent answers scheduling, refill and billing calls around the clock. It depends on the contact center platform, a speech model, identity checks and the EHR's scheduling interface all working together.

today.title: Routine calls move to an agent
today.exec: The agent takes routine calls at any hour, so patient access now depends on a chain of cloud services the hospital does not run.
today.dir: The telephony carrier, contact center platform, speech and language models and the EHR interface each have a different owner and status page.
today.eng: A call crosses SIP trunks, the contact center platform, speech-to-text, a language model and EHR API calls; added latency in any hop is audible to the caller.

today.title: The booking that never reached the schedule
today.exec: A caller hears a confirmation, the write to the schedule fails silently, and the patient arrives for an appointment that does not exist.
today.dir: Containment dashboards count the call as resolved, so the failure surfaces as complaints, not as an alert.
today.eng: Nothing reconciles the agent's confirmations against EHR write-back responses or the interface error queue.

today.title: Identity and handoff are the weak points
today.exec: A caller who is not who they claim to be can reach refill or billing details, and a distressed caller can loop instead of reaching a person.
today.dir: Identity checks and transfer rules are configured in the vendor's console, outside the hospital's change control.
today.eng: Agent service accounts often hold broad EHR scopes, and transfers lose context when the staffed queue and the agent platform do not share session data.

withCisco.title: One investigation across the call path
withCisco.exec: One investigation shows the call path, the agent's steps and the EHR interface together, so the team sees where bookings stop.
withCisco.dir: AI Canvas would combine contact center data (Webex Contact Center where deployed), ThousandEyes tests to the model and EHR endpoints, and Splunk logs.
withCisco.eng: Agent Observability would trace each agent step and tool call, ThousandEyes would measure voice and API paths, and Splunk would join write-back errors to call records.

withCisco.title: A person approves the failover
withCisco.exec: Before calls are rerouted to staff or the agent's permissions are narrowed, the patient access director approves the change and sees who is affected.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the routing change for approval and the Audit log would keep the record.
withCisco.eng: The approved change runs in the contact center platform's routing configuration; Duo would verify the approver.

withCisco.title: Modeled: failed bookings caught the same day
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: silent booking failures are caught the same day instead of at the front desk; the agent's accuracy and tone stay the vendor's to fix.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes the agent vendor exposes traces and the EHR interface logs are searchable; many vendors do not expose both.
withCisco.eng: Third-party agent platforms are visible only through their telemetry exports and from network path tests.

approval.title: Reroute calls from agent to staff
approval.what: Send scheduling calls to the staffed queue and suspend the agent's booking permission until write-back errors clear.
approval.executesIn: Contact center platform routing (Webex Contact Center where deployed)

ask: How would you find out that your phone agent confirmed appointments last night that never reached the schedule?
stays: The agent's script, voice, accuracy and identity-verification method stay with the agent vendor and patient access; EHR scopes stay with the EHR team.
caveat: Call volumes and containment rates here are vendor-reported, with no independent audit found. The Cisco story is a hypothesis about visibility and approval, and the outcome is modeled.

title: The hospital buys its own GPUs
subtitle: To keep patient data in-house and costs predictable, a health system installs a GPU cluster for language and imaging models in a data center built for far lighter racks.

today.title: Research hardware becomes clinical infrastructure
today.exec: A cluster bought for research starts serving models that clinicians use daily, without the uptime design or staffing of a clinical system.
today.dir: Ownership is split between research computing, infrastructure and data science, and none runs an on-call rota for model serving.
today.eng: GPU nodes, a low-loss east-west fabric, shared storage and the inference serving stack are managed in separate tools with separate firmware cycles.

today.title: Power and cooling set the ceiling
today.exec: A current GPU rack can draw more than ten times a typical rack, so facilities limits, not budget, decide how much AI the hospital can run.
today.dir: Capacity planning for GPUs, power and cooling lives in spreadsheets, and requests from clinical teams queue without a shared view.
today.eng: Racks of 120 to 132 kW need liquid cooling, against an industry average near 9 kW per rack.

today.title: A slow model looks like a broken app
today.exec: When the cluster is saturated or a node fails, clinicians see a slow or failed tool, and nobody can say quickly which layer is at fault.
today.dir: The application team blames the model, the model team blames the cluster, and the cluster team has no view of the application.
today.eng: Fabric congestion or a failing optic shows up as slow tokens and timeouts, not as a link-down alarm.

withCisco.title: One view from GPU to clinical app
withCisco.exec: One investigation shows GPU load, fabric health, storage and the applications that depend on the cluster in a single view.
withCisco.dir: AI Canvas would bring Intersight compute and GPU telemetry, Nexus fabric data and Splunk application logs into one investigation.
withCisco.eng: Intersight would report node, GPU and firmware state, Nexus telemetry would show fabric congestion, and Splunk would correlate inference latency with both.

withCisco.title: Approval before clinical workloads move
withCisco.exec: Before a node is drained or a clinical model is moved, the infrastructure lead and the model's clinical owner approve the change and its timing.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the change for both approvers and the Audit log would record the decision.
withCisco.eng: The approved action executes in Intersight (firmware, node maintenance) or the Nexus controller, not from the agent.

withCisco.title: Modeled: saturation seen before clinicians feel it
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: saturation is seen before clinicians feel it; power, cooling, model quality and who staffs the platform remain the hospital's decisions.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes Cisco compute and fabric; clusters built on other vendors' hardware would appear only through Splunk data.
withCisco.eng: Model-serving software, schedulers and the models themselves are outside Intersight and Nexus telemetry, and AI Defense would test models for safety and security issues, not for uptime.

approval.what: Drain one node for a firmware fix and shift imaging inference to the remaining nodes during the overnight window.
approval.approver: Infrastructure lead with the clinical AI owner

ask: Who is on call at 2 a.m. for the GPU cluster your clinicians now depend on, and what would they look at first?
stays: Power and cooling build-out, the choice of models, clinical validation and the staffing of the platform team stay with the hospital and its facilities partners.
caveat: No statistic on how many hospitals run their own GPU clusters was found; published examples are surveys and implementation reports, not outcome studies. What Cisco products would show is a hypothesis; the outcome is modeled.

title: A sepsis score depends on fresh data
subtitle: A deterioration model scores every inpatient from vitals, labs and notes. If a feed from monitors or the lab lags, the score goes stale and nurses see alerts they stop trusting.

today.title: The model reads feeds nobody watches
today.exec: The score depends on monitor, lab and EHR feeds arriving on time, and those feeds are watched as interfaces, not as a clinical dependency.
today.dir: The interface engine, device gateways and the model runtime belong to three teams; the model owner sees scores, not feed latency.
today.eng: Vitals arrive through device integration gateways and HL7 or FHIR interfaces; a queue backlog delays model inputs without raising an error to the model.

today.title: Stale inputs, confident output
today.exec: When a feed lags, the model still produces a score, so a patient can look stable on screen while the latest readings are missing.
today.dir: No dashboard shows clinicians or IT how old the inputs behind a given score are.
today.eng: Most deployed models do not expose input freshness, so a missing lab or delayed vitals batch changes the score silently.

today.title: Alerts fire late or too often
today.exec: Even the updated sepsis model, validated at four health systems in 2026, kept a low positive predictive value and a high alert burden, varying by site.
today.dir: Alert fatigue rises, and with ONC's model-card requirement removed from December 28, 2026, local monitoring falls to the hospital.
today.eng: Model drift, data-quality drift and pipeline latency cannot be told apart unless input timestamps are logged next to each prediction.

withCisco.title: One view of the data path
withCisco.exec: One investigation shows whether monitors, the network, the interface engine and the model host are delivering data on time.
withCisco.dir: AI Canvas would join Catalyst Center network telemetry with interface-engine and model-host logs in Splunk, using Federated Search for data left in place.
withCisco.eng: Splunk would hold interface queue depth and message timestamps, Topology would show gateway connectivity, and Federated Search would reach logs kept in other stores.

withCisco.title: Clinical informatics approves any change
withCisco.exec: Any change that could alter alerts at the bedside, such as restarting an interface or rerouting a gateway, waits for clinical informatics approval.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the request and the Audit log would record the approver and the window agreed with the unit.
withCisco.eng: Network changes run in Catalyst Center; interface-engine restarts run in the hospital's own interface tooling through its change system.

withCisco.title: Modeled: stale feeds flagged, accuracy unchanged
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: a lagging feed is flagged before scores go stale; the model's accuracy, thresholds and alert fatigue remain a clinical governance matter.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes interface-engine and model-host logs are sent to Splunk or retained in Machine Data Lake, which is integration work the hospital must do.
withCisco.eng: Nothing here validates the model; it only shows whether the inputs arrived and when.

approval.what: Restart the monitor-to-EHR interface channel and replay queued vitals for two units in a window agreed with charge nurses.

ask: For your sepsis or deterioration score, can anyone tell you right now how old the newest vitals and labs behind it are?
stays: Model choice, thresholds, validation, alert design and the clinical response stay with clinical governance and the model vendor.
caveat: The updated model discriminates better than the first, but alert burden stays high. No published measurement of feed latency for these models was found. Infrastructure visibility does not make a model accurate; the outcome shown is modeled.

title: Every agent in the chart needs an identity
subtitle: Agents built in the EHR, by revenue-cycle vendors and by staff now read and write clinical systems. Few hospitals can list them, their permissions or what they did last night.

today.title: Agents arrive from three directions
today.exec: EHR vendor agents, revenue-cycle agents and staff-built agents all gain access to patient data, each approved through a different door.
today.dir: There is no single register of agents, owners, permissions and credentials, and service accounts are shared and rarely expire.
today.eng: Agents authenticate with OAuth client credentials, SMART on FHIR backend services or API keys, and MCP servers add a tool layer with its own authorization.

today.title: Permissions wider than the task
today.exec: An agent set up to check claim status can hold access broad enough to read whole charts, because narrowing it is work nobody owns.
today.dir: Access reviews cover people; agent credentials are reviewed, if at all, when a vendor contract renews.
today.eng: Scopes are granted per integration, not per task, and tokens are long-lived.

today.title: An injected instruction acts with real access
today.exec: Text hidden in a document or message can redirect an agent, and the audit trail shows a service account, not which agent acted or why.
today.dir: In a published test, prompt injection succeeded in 94.4% of simulated medical-advice dialogues.
today.eng: EHR audit logs record the API client; the agent's reasoning, tool calls and the prompt that triggered them live in a separate system or nowhere.

withCisco.title: One register of agents and their reach
withCisco.exec: One view lists agents, their identities, the systems they reach and their recent actions, drawn from identity, network and agent telemetry.
withCisco.dir: Cisco Identity would bring identity and agentic activity into one view, Duo would verify approvers, AI Defense would discover and test AI assets, and Agent Observability would trace agent behavior.
withCisco.eng: Secure Access would apply per-agent policy to MCP and API traffic, with traces, tool calls and guardrail events held in Splunk.

withCisco.title: A named owner approves each permission change
withCisco.exec: Granting an agent write access, or suspending one that misbehaves, requires approval from the agent's named owner and from security.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the request and the Audit log would tie the decision to a person.
withCisco.eng: Network-side blocks execute in Secure Access; EHR-side permissions are changed in the EHR vendor's console by the EHR team.

withCisco.title: Modeled: a misbehaving agent stopped, with a record
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: a misbehaving agent is identified and suspended with a full record; what agents may do inside the EHR stays with the EHR vendor and hospital governance.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes agents are registered and their traffic passes through enforced paths; agents embedded inside the EHR are visible only through the vendor's own logs.
withCisco.eng: Guardrails reduce prompt-injection risk; they do not remove it.

approval.title: Suspend an agent's access to records
approval.what: Block the prior-authorization agent's API traffic and request removal of its write permission until its owner reviews the flagged actions.
approval.approver: Security lead with the agent's business owner
approval.executesIn: Cisco Secure Access; EHR vendor console for EHR-side permissions

ask: Could you list tonight every AI agent that can read or write your EHR, who owns each one, and what it did yesterday?
stays: What agents may do inside the EHR, clinical sign-off rules and each vendor's agent design stay with the EHR vendor, the agent vendors and hospital AI governance.
caveat: No healthcare survey of agent identities and no red-team of an agent with live EHR write access was found; identity ratios are cross-industry and vendor-reported. Cisco capabilities here are hypotheses, and the outcome is modeled.

title: Every glass slide becomes gigabytes on the network
subtitle: The lab scans every slide so pathologists and AI can read them anywhere. Each slide is gigabytes, and scanners, storage, links between sites and the cloud must all keep pace.

today.title: Scanners outrun the network plan
today.exec: Digitizing the lab turns a courier problem into a data problem: each slide is gigabytes, every day, kept for years.
today.dir: Scanner purchases are led by pathology; storage growth, WAN capacity and cloud transfer costs are discovered after go-live.
today.eng: Scanners write multi-gigabyte image files to an image management system, and viewers stream tiles, so latency and loss show up as slow pan and zoom.

today.title: A slow viewer means a waiting diagnosis
today.exec: When a link between sites or to the cloud degrades, pathologists wait for images and cases queue, cancer cases included.
today.dir: The lab reports the viewer is slow; the network, storage and cloud teams each see green.
today.eng: Tile streaming is sensitive to round-trip time, and bulk archive jobs compete with interactive viewing on the same circuits.

today.title: AI results depend on the whole chain
today.exec: AI tools need each slide to arrive complete and on time; a stalled transfer or a full storage tier delays the result without a clear alarm.
today.dir: Few AI algorithms are cleared, each tied to specific scanners and viewers, so every site-to-site move must preserve a validated chain.
today.eng: Failed or partial transfers surface as missing AI overlays in the viewer, with the cause in transfer or storage logs.

withCisco.title: One view from scanner to archive
withCisco.exec: One investigation shows scanner connectivity, the links between sites, the cloud path and storage-side errors together.
withCisco.dir: AI Canvas would combine Catalyst SD-WAN path data, ThousandEyes tests to the cloud archive, Nexus and Intersight data-center telemetry and Splunk logs.
withCisco.eng: ThousandEyes would measure loss and latency to the image archive, Catalyst SD-WAN would show per-application path choice, and Splunk would hold transfer and storage logs.

withCisco.title: The lab director approves traffic changes
withCisco.exec: Before slide traffic is rerouted or a transfer window is moved, the lab's medical director and the network lead approve it.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the change and the Audit log would record the approval for the lab's quality file.
withCisco.eng: Approved policy changes are executed by the Catalyst SD-WAN controller, not by the agent.

withCisco.title: Modeled: a degrading path found before sign-out slips
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: a degrading path is found before sign-out slips; storage cost, retention policy and AI validation stay with the lab and its vendors.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes the image management vendor's logs can be collected; some are closed.
withCisco.eng: Scanner throughput, compression and viewer performance are outside network telemetry.

approval.what: Move whole-slide transfers from the degraded circuit to the secondary path and reschedule the bulk archive job overnight.

ask: When a pathologist says the viewer is slow, how long does it take to learn whether it is the scanner, the link, the cloud or the storage?
stays: Scanner and viewer validation, slide retention policy, storage spend and the choice of AI algorithms stay with the laboratory and its vendors.
caveat: No peer-reviewed 2025 to 2026 figure for end-to-end turnaround from pathology AI or for petabyte-scale storage was found. Network visibility does not validate a diagnostic chain, and the outcome shown is modeled.

title: Nobody can say what the AI costs
subtitle: Scribes, agents, imaging tools and a GPU cluster each bill differently: per user, per token, per study, per watt. Finance sees invoices; IT sees usage; no one sees both.

today.title: AI spend moves from seats to tokens
today.exec: AI is increasingly billed by consumption, so cost rises with every agent step and no longer tracks headcount or licenses.
today.dir: Budgets are set per contract, while usage is driven by workflows nobody forecasts.
today.eng: Token counts, model choice, retries and agent loops drive cost; without per-request telemetry tagged to an application, spend cannot be attributed.

today.title: Tools multiply faster than oversight
today.exec: Each department adds AI tools, and IT spends a growing share of its time on vendors and integrations instead of outcomes.
today.dir: In a 2026 vendor-run survey, 51% of health-system IT leaders spent 11% to 25% of IT bandwidth on vendor management, integrations and implementations.
today.eng: Overlapping tools call different models through different gateways, so there is no common usage record.

today.title: Value is asserted, not measured
today.exec: Leaders approve more AI spend while few can tie it to measured results, so the next budget cycle is argued on anecdotes.
today.dir: Only 18% of AI-scaling organizations in a 2026 healthcare CFO survey reported mature financial attribution.
today.eng: Before-and-after comparisons stand in for attribution because usage, cost and outcome data sit in different systems.

withCisco.title: One view of usage, capacity and cost drivers
withCisco.exec: One view shows which applications and agents consume tokens and GPU time, alongside the infrastructure they run on.
withCisco.dir: In AI Canvas, Agent Observability would report token use and cost per agent, Intersight would report GPU utilization, and Splunk with Machine Data Lake would keep the usage history.
withCisco.eng: Agent traces carry token and model metadata; Intersight exposes GPU utilization per node; Machine Data Lake retains the raw records for later attribution.

withCisco.title: The AI program owner approves limits
withCisco.exec: A cap on an agent's usage, or a move to a cheaper model, is approved by the AI program owner, with clinical sign-off where care is touched.
withCisco.dir: The Actions queue would hold the change and the Audit log would record who accepted the trade-off.
withCisco.eng: The limit is applied in the agent platform or model gateway; Cisco tooling records the request, the approval and the usage afterwards.

withCisco.title: Modeled: spend attributed by application
withCisco.exec: Modeled outcome: spend is attributed to applications and owners each month; whether the AI is worth it is still a clinical and financial judgment.
withCisco.dir: The model assumes vendors expose usage data; per-seat SaaS tools often expose none.
withCisco.eng: Vendor invoices and contract terms are not in machine telemetry and must be joined from finance systems.

ask: If your AI bill doubled next quarter, could you say which application, which agent and which department drove it?
stays: Contracts, pricing, the decision to keep or retire a tool and the measure of clinical value stay with finance, clinical leaders and each vendor.
caveat: No health-system figure for token or inference spend was found; cost-control statistics are cross-industry and vendor-reported. Cisco tooling would show usage, not value, and the outcome is modeled.
